tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Give helper functions a new Verb-Noun name such as Read-Doc, also in script files. A built-in alias (rd, rm, del, ri, sc, mv and others) runs instead of a function with the same name, with no warning.
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
    - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings

When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

<pasted_content id="e988">
Poniższe punkty wskazują, co należy ustalić, wykonać i sprawdzić. Nie są listą osobnych poleceń do agenta. Po rozpoznaniu projektu możesz jednym zleceniem powierzyć mu sprawdzenie środowiska, uruchomienie skryptu, odczyt raportu i test. Nie jest wymagany osobny dokument z planem.
1. Rozpoznaj projekt i określ zlecenie#

Poproś agenta, żeby na podstawie README wyjaśnił działanie describe_data.py i wskazał instrukcję uruchomienia. Odszukaj odczyt tego fragmentu w sesji. Obejrzyj jedną wiadomość z project/data/exercise.csv i ustal znaczenie pól message_id, text i label.

Przed wykonaniem określ w rozmowie:

    Wynik: raport dla project/data/exercise.csv, zapisany w project/results/exercise-summary.json.
    Granice: w etapie 1 bez zmian kodu, danych i testów. Etap 2 dopuszcza zmianę jednej etykiety i odświeżenie raportu.
    Odbiór: agent ma wskazać miejsce raportu, odczytać jego treść oraz pokazać użyte dane, wykonane polecenie i wynik procesu. Ma też podać wynik testu i zgłosić ewentualne niewykonane kroki.

Możesz korzystać z propozycji agenta. Przed zleceniem wykonania upewnij się, że rozumiesz i przyjmujesz ten zakres.
2. Wyjaśnij jeden fragment#

Wybierz krótki fragment README lub kodu związany z tym zadaniem. Z pomocą agenta wyjaśnij jego znaczenie, a następnie opisz je własnymi słowami. Poproś o mały, zmieniony przypadek dotyczący tego samego mechanizmu; przewidź skutek przed poznaniem odpowiedzi. Sprawdź przewidywanie w dokumentacji, kodzie lub bezpiecznej próbie i wyjaśnij ewentualną różnicę. Nie zmieniaj plików projektu na potrzeby tego ćwiczenia.

Nie musisz analizować całego skryptu ani kodu testu. Fragment powinien pomagać zrozumieć wykonanie lub wynik, a nie służyć zapamiętywaniu składni.
3. Zleć wykonanie i odczyt raportu#

Zleć agentowi sprawdzenie katalogu roboczego i wersji Pythona, wykonanie skryptu zgodnie z README oraz odczyt zapisanego raportu. Ustal, czy polecenia wykonuje Twój komputer, czy inne środowisko udostępnione przez aplikację.

Odszukaj rzeczywiste wywołanie i wynik procesu. Wyjaśnij podział ról: model wybiera polecenie → aplikacja obsługuje narzędzie → komputer wykonuje skrypt → wynik wraca do modelu. Sam tekst komendy lub odpowiedź „gotowe” nie potwierdza wykonania.
4. Odbierz wynik#

Sprawdź miejsce zapisu, porównaj input_file z wejściem podanym w poleceniu i wyjaśnij liczebności w raporcie. Powiąż odczytany raport z zakończonym uruchomieniem; sam istniejący plik może pochodzić z wcześniejszej próby. Zachowaj jego treść w sesji do porównania z etapem 2.

Pomocniczo możesz porównać liczebności z etykietami w CSV. Ręczne liczenie wszystkich wiadomości nie jest wymagane. Jeśli wykonanie się nie udało, nie przedstawiaj starego raportu jako nowego wyniku. Ustal przyczynę z agentem; w razie blokady zgłoś prowadzącemu polecenie, komunikat i niewykonany krok.
5. Odczytaj wynik gotowego testu#

Zleć uruchomienie testu poleceniem z README, jeśli nie zostało już objęte wspólnym zleceniem. Odszukaj jego wywołanie i wynik. Z pomocą agenta ustal, jakie dane test wykorzystuje i co porównuje; wyjaśnij to własnymi słowami.

Test uruchamia skrypt na osobnych wiadomościach i porównuje utworzony raport z oczekiwaniem. Nie odczytuje exercise-summary.json. Nie musisz analizować porównań w kodzie testu ani go modyfikować. Jeśli test się nie powiedzie, poproś o wyjaśnienie komunikatu; nie zmieniaj oczekiwań, żeby uzyskać powodzenie.

1	# First run — SpamAssassin messages
2	
3	This is the starting point for a spam classification project. Your task is to **run the prepared Python script `describe_data.py` with a coding agent, confirm the origin of its report, and run the supplied test on an example with known expected results**. The program counts existing dataset labels; it does not train a model or run the Apache SpamAssassin spam filter.
4	
5	## Files
6	
7	| File | Purpose |
8	|---|---|
9	| `describe_data.py` | Read a CSV, count messages and labels, and save a JSON report. |
10	| `tests/test_report.py` | Run the program and check the saved report against known expected values. |
11	| `tests/fixtures/messages.csv` | Three synthetic messages used only by the test, not from SpamAssassin. |
12	| `data/demo.csv` | Optional sample messages. |
13	| `data/exercise.csv` | Messages for your exercise. |
14	| `data/raw/<message_id>.eml` | Original messages, available to inspect as plain text. |
15	| [data/README.md](data/README.md) | Field definitions, sources, and data preparation. |
16	| `data/manifest.json` | Links to the source messages and file checksums. |
17	
18	One CSV record represents one email. The `text` field contains its subject and full body, which can span multiple lines. **Counting physical lines in the CSV does not count messages.** `spam` means unwanted email; `ham` means legitimate email according to the dataset label. The identifier links a record to its original message.
19	
20	Inspect one message to understand the fields. You do not need to understand the technical discussions inside the emails or decide whether their labels are correct. Manually counting all labels is optional; the main task is to run the program and trace the saved result to its execution.
21	
22	## Environment and first run
23	
24	You need Python 3.10 or later and a coding-agent application with a tool that can run terminal commands in the project directory. The script uses only Python's standard library: no `pip` packages, downloads, or GPU are required.
25	
26	1. Open this `project` folder in the agent application using the course setup instructions. Ask the agent to explain what `describe_data.py` reads and writes, pointing to the relevant files. Before running it, identify the intended input and output paths in the session. Ask about unfamiliar terms.
27	2. Ask the agent to check its working directory and run `python3 --version` (Windows: `py -3 --version`). Find the actual command and result in the session. Identify whether it ran on your computer or in another environment provided by the application. Python must be available there. If a command fails, use the instructions and the agent's help; report the specific blocker if you cannot resolve it.
28	3. Ask the agent to execute:
29	
30	   ```bash
31	   python3 describe_data.py --data data/exercise.csv --out results/exercise-summary.json

# First run — SpamAssassin messages

This is the starting point for a spam classification project. Your task is to **run the prepared Python script `describe_data.py` with a coding agent, confirm the origin of its report, and run the supplied test on an example with known expected results**. | `data/demo.csv` | Optional sample messages. |
| `data/exercise.csv` | Messages for your exercise. |
| `data/raw/<message_id>.eml` | Original messages, available to inspect as plain text. |
| [data/README.md](data/README.md) | Field definitions, sources, and data preparation. |
| `data/manifest.json` | Links to the source messages and file checksums. |

One CSV record represents one email. The `text` field contains its subject and full body, which can span multiple lines. **Counting physical lines in the CSV does not count messages.** `spam` means unwanted email; `ham` means legitimate email according to the dataset label. The identifier links a record to its original message.

1	"""Summarize message labels in a CSV file and save a run report."""
2	
3	import argparse
4	import csv
5	import hashlib
6	import io
7	import json
8	from pathlib import Path
9	import platform
10	import sys
11	
12	
13	def describe(input_path):
14	    raw = input_path.read_bytes()
15	    rows = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw.decode("utf-8"), newline=""))
16	    if rows.fieldnames != ["message_id", "text", "label"]:
17	        raise ValueError("Expected columns: message_id,text,label.")
18	
19	    counts = {"ham": 0, "spam": 0}
20	    seen_ids = set()
21	    for number, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):
22	        if None in row or any(not value or not value.strip() for value in row.values()):
23	            raise ValueError(f"Record {number}: missing or extra field.")
24	        if row["message_id"] in seen_ids:
25	            raise ValueError(f"Record {number}: duplicate message_id.")
26	        if row["label"] not in counts:
27	            raise ValueError(f"Record {number}: label must be ham or spam.")
28	        seen_ids.add(row["message_id"])
29	        counts[row["label"]] += 1
30	
31	    if not seen_ids:
32	        raise ValueError("The file contains no messages.")
33	
34	    return {
35	        "input_file": str(input_path.resolve()),
36	        "input_sha256": hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest(),
37	        "total_messages": sum(counts.values()),
38	        "label_counts": counts,
39	        "runtime": {
40	            "python_executable": sys.executable,
41	            "python_version": platform.python_version(),
42	            "working_directory": str(Path.cwd()),
43	        },
44	    }
45	
46	
47	def main():
48	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
49	    parser.add_argument("--data", type=Path, required=True, help="Input CSV file")
50	    parser.add_argument("--out", type=Path, required=True, help="Output JSON report")
51	    args = parser.parse_args()
52	    if args.data.resolve() == args.out.resolve():
53	        parser.error("The report must be a different file from the input data.")
54	
55	    try:
56	        report = describe(args.data)
57	        args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
58	        args.out.write_text(
59	            json.dumps(report, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
60	        )
61	    except (OSError, UnicodeError, csv.Error, ValueError) as error:
62	        parser.exit(1, f"Error: {error}\n")
63	
64	    print(f"Report saved: {args.out.resolve()}")
65	    print(f"Messages: {report['total_messages']}; labels: {report['label_counts']}")
66	
67	
68	if __name__ == "__main__":
69	    main()
70

The subject, body transfer encoding, and declared character encoding were decoded (ASCII when no charset was declared). Line endings were normalized to LF. Bodies were not truncated; quotations and footers were retained.
23	3. The `text` field was assembled as `Subject: <subject>`, two newlines, and the body. Other headers remain in the original `.eml` file, but are not included in the CSV.
24	4. Labels came from the archive directory: `easy_ham` → `ham`, `spam` → `spam`. Local identifiers were assigned, and the CSV files were saved as UTF-8 with LF line endings.
25	
26	`manifest.json` records archive URLs and SHA-256 hashes, selected archive members, their `.eml` paths, and hashes of the originals and CSV packets. It supports reproducing the selection and checking it against the same archives. Filenames, identifiers, and labels are not input features for the future model.
27	
28	## Usage terms

30	According to the [corpus description](https://spamassassin.apache.org/old/publiccorpus/readme.html), copyright in the message texts remains with the original senders. The SpamAssassin software license is not a license for these messages. The publisher instructs users not to send them through a live email system. In this project, we read files as text; we do not send the messages or open their links.

Poniżej punkt 1. Przeczytałem tylko te pliki: `project/README.md`, `project/data/README.md`, `project/describe_data.py` i pierwszy rekord `project/data/exercise.csv`. Niczego nie uruchomiłem ani nie zmieniłem.

## Co robi `describe_data.py`

Według README skrypt liczy etykiety, które już są w danych. Nie trenuje modelu i nie uruchamia filtra SpamAssassin (`project/README.md:3`).

- **Co czyta:** plik CSV podany w `--data` (`describe_data.py:49`). Wymaga dokładnie kolumn `message_id,text,label` (`:16`).
- **Co sprawdza w każdym rekordzie:** czy żadne pole nie jest puste ani nie ma pól nadmiarowych (`:22`), czy `message_id` się nie powtarza (`:24`) i czy etykieta to `ham` albo `spam` (`:26`). Pusty plik też kończy się błędem (`:31`).
- **Co zapisuje:** raport JSON w ścieżce `--out` (`:50`, `:58`). Sam tworzy brakujący katalog (`:57`). Nadpisuje wcześniejszy raport. Nie pozwala, żeby wejście i wyjście były tym samym plikiem (`:52`).
- **Co jest w raporcie:**
  - `input_file`: ścieżka bezwzględna wejścia
  - `input_sha256`: suma kontrolna wejścia
  - `total_messages`: liczba wiadomości
  - `label_counts`: liczba `ham` i `spam`
  - `runtime`: interpreter, wersja Pythona i katalog roboczy
- **Na końcu:** wypisuje `Report saved: ...` oraz liczebności (`:64-65`). Przy błędzie wypisuje `Error: ...` i kończy z kodem 1 (`:62`). Stary raport zostaje wtedy na dysku.

## Instrukcja uruchomienia (`project/README.md:28-34`, `:56-60`)

Polecenia wykonuje się z katalogu `project`. Na Windowsie zamiast `python3` jest `py -3`:

```
py -3 --version
py -3 describe_data.py --data data/exercise.csv --out results/exercise-summary.json
py -3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

## Jedna wiadomość: `exercise-001` (wiersze 2–24 CSV)

```
exercise-001,"Subject: [SAdev] Interesting approach to Spam handling..

Hello, have you seen and discussed this article and his approach?
...
Spamassassin-devel mailing list
...
",ham
```

- **`message_id`** = `exercise-001`. To identyfikator w tym pakiecie danych. Łączy rekord z oryginałem `data/raw/exercise-001.eml`.
- **`text`** to temat (`Subject: ...`), pusta linia i cała treść. Ten jeden rekord zajmuje w pliku 23 linie, bo treść ma akapity. Dlatego liczenie linii nie daje liczby wiadomości.
- **`label`** = `ham`, czyli legalna wiadomość. Etykieta pochodzi z korpusu źródłowego, a nie ze skryptu. Ta wiadomość zawiera reklamową stopkę („Get a new here for FREE!”), a mimo to jest oznaczona jako `ham`. Tak jak ostrzega `data/README.md:11`, nie należy oceniać etykiety po pojedynczym słowie.

## Proponowany zakres zlecenia

- **Wynik:** raport dla `project/data/exercise.csv` zapisany w `project/results/exercise-summary.json`.
- **Granice:** w etapie 1 bez zmian w kodzie, danych i testach. Etap 2 dopuszcza zmianę jednej etykiety i odświeżenie raportu.
- **Odbiór:** agent:
  - wskazuje, gdzie zapisał raport, i odczytuje jego treść,
  - pokazuje użyte dane, wykonane polecenie i wynik procesu (wydruk i kod wyjścia),
  - podaje wynik testu,
  - zgłasza kroki, których nie wykonał.

Do porównania w punkcie 4: plik ma 8 rekordów z etykietą na końcu, 5 `ham` i 3 `spam`. Sprawdziłem to wyszukiwaniem, a nie uruchomieniem skryptu.

Czy przyjmujesz ten zakres? Jeśli tak, przejdziemy do punktu 2, czyli wyjaśnienia jednego fragmentu.

content.text:
Do odbioru dopisuję dwa punkty: kod wyjścia każdego polecenia oraz to, czy polecenia wykonał Twój komputer, czy inne środowisko.

## Fragment `describe_data.py:55-62`

```python
try:
    report = describe(args.data)                       # 1. czyta i sprawdza cały plik, buduje raport w pamięci
    args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) # 2. tworzy katalog wyjściowy
    args.out.write_text(json.dumps(report, ...) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")  # 3. zapisuje JSON
except (OSError, UnicodeError, csv.Error, ValueError) as error:
    parser.exit(1, f"Error: {error}\n")                # komunikat na stderr, kod wyjścia 1
```

**Kolejność.** Najpierw `describe()` przechodzi przez cały plik CSV i składa gotowy słownik z raportem, ale tylko w pamięci. Dopiero gdy całe sprawdzanie się uda, skrypt tworzy katalog i zapisuje plik. Jeśli `describe()` przerwie pracę wyjątkiem, kroki 2 i 3 w ogóle się nie wykonają.

**Obsługa błędu.** Skrypt przechwytuje cztery rodzaje błędów:
- `OSError`: brak pliku albo brak prawa do zapisu,
- `UnicodeError`: plik nie jest w UTF-8,
- `csv.Error`: uszkodzony CSV,
- `ValueError`: błędy z własnych sprawdzeń, na przykład zła etykieta, duplikat albo brakujące pole.

W każdym z tych przypadków `parser.exit(1, ...)` wypisuje `Error: ...` i kończy proces z kodem 1. Linie 64–65 (`Report saved: ...`) się wtedy nie wykonują.

**Skutek praktyczny.** Nieudany przebieg nie zostawia częściowego raportu, ale też nie usuwa starego. Dlatego sama obecność `exercise-summary.json` nie dowodzi, że ostatnie uruchomienie się udało. Trzeba patrzeć na kod wyjścia i wydruk.

## Twoja kolej

1. Opisz ten fragment własnymi słowami.
2. Potem przewidź wynik zmienionego przypadku poniżej. Odpowiedzi jeszcze nie podaję.

**Przypadek:** `results/exercise-summary.json` istnieje już z udanego wcześniejszego przebiegu, z liczebnościami 5 `ham` i 3 `spam`. Uruchamiamy skrypt z tym samym `--out` na kopii `exercise.csv`, w której 6. rekord ma etykietę `Spam` (wielką literą), a pozostałe są bez zmian.

Przewidź:
- co wypisze skrypt,
- jaki będzie kod wyjścia,
- co będzie w pliku raportu po tym przebiegu: stara treść, nowa, plik pusty czy brak pliku?

Swoje przewidywanie sprawdzimy potem bezpieczną próbą. Kopia danych i raport trafią wyłącznie do katalogu tymczasowego (scratchpad), więc nie zmienię niczego w `project/`. Jeśli wolisz, sprawdzimy to tylko na podstawie kodu.

"""Check a saved report using three synthetic messages: two ham and one spam."""

import json
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import unittest


PROJECT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
FIXTURE = PROJECT / "tests" / "fixtures" / "messages.csv"


class ReportTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_cli_writes_expected_counts(self):
        """The CLI saves a report for the intended input with counts 3 / 2 / 1."""
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="spam-lab-test-") as directory:
            output = Path(directory) / "summary.json"
            result = subprocess.run(
                [sys.executable, str(PROJECT / "describe_data.py"),
                 "--data", str(FIXTURE), "--out", str(output)],
                cwd=PROJECT,
                capture_output=True,
                text=True,
            )
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 0, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            self.assertTrue(output.is_file(), "The program did not save a report.")
            report = json.loads(output.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
            self.assertEqual(report["input_file"], str(FIXTURE))
            self.assertEqual(report["total_messages"], 3)
            self.assertEqual(report["label_counts"], {"ham": 2, "spam": 1})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

exercise-004,"Subject: [ILUG] Re: Problems with RAID1 on cobalt raq3

On Mon, Aug 19, 2002 at 03:08:16PM +0100, John P. Looney mentioned:
>  This is likely because to get it to boot, like the cobalt, I'm actually
> passing root=/dev/hda5 to the kernel, not /dev/md0. 

 Just to solve this...the reason I was booting the box with
root=/dev/hda5, not /dev/md0 was because /dev/md0 wasn't booting - it
would barf with 'can't find init'.

 It turns out that this is because I was populating md0 with tar. Which
seems to have 'issues' with crosslinked files - for instance, it was
trying to make a hard link of glibc.so to hda - and failing. It was only
as I did it again with a friend present, that he spotted the errors, and
queried them. We noticed that the hard linked files just didn't exist on
the new rootfs.

 When we duplicated the filesystems with dump instead of tar, it worked
fine, I was able to tell lilo to use root=/dev/md0 and everything worked.

 Woohoo.

Kate
